description: The figure presents three pie charts—labeled “easy,” “medium,” and “hard”—showing the distribution of problem outcomes under CoT (Chain-of-Thought) reasoning, categorized by whether the model had access to knowledge (K) and whether it arrived at the correct answer (N), with four combinations: N+K+ (correct with knowledge, teal), N−K+ (incorrect despite having knowledge, yellow), N−K− (incorrect without knowledge, orange), and N+K− (correct without knowledge, red). In the “easy” chart, N−K+ dominates at 45.9%, followed by N+K+ at 40.6%, with smaller shares for N−K− (10.1%) and N+K− (3.3%). The “medium” chart shows near parity between N+K+ (44.6%) and N−K+ (44.3%), with N−K− at 7.2% and N+K− at 3.9%. In the “hard” chart, N−K− becomes the largest segment at 36.8%, followed by N−K+ at 36.2%, N+K+ drops sharply to 20.1%, and N+K− is minimal at 7.0%. A legend on the right identifies the color coding for each category, and all percentages are labeled directly on the slices. The visual progression across difficulty levels suggests that as problems become harder, the model’s ability to leverage knowledge for correct answers diminishes, while reasoning failures (N−K−) become increasingly prevalent.
caption_used: Problem distribution based on correctness under the w/ knowledge and w/o knowledge settings using CoT. The results indicate that while easier problems are primarily hindered by a lack of knowledge (N−K+ at approximately 50%), medium problems show a consistent dominance of reasoning-based errors (N−K− at 15%). For hard problems, the primary bottleneck lies in the inability to integrate geometric reasoning, as evidenced by the sharp decline in N+K+ to below 10%.
